pack.name: Business Ethics
pack.title: The Weighing of Souls
pack.blurb: Moral philosophy, scandals, fallacies, watchdogs and doing the right thing.

prompts.text: Name a moral philosopher or ethical thinker.
prompts.flavor: They asked what a good life is. Whatever answered them from the dark was very patient.
prompts.rules: Any philosopher, religious teacher or writer known for ideas about right and wrong, from any age or tradition. Surnames alone are fine.

answers.lore: In the 400s BC he taught impartial care for everyone and judged every policy by its benefit to the people: utilitarianism, two thousand years early.
The ancient Chinese egoist who, Mencius complained, would not pluck out one hair from his body to benefit the whole world.
She gave up a rich family in about 325 BC to live on the streets of Athens as a Cynic philosopher with her husband Crates.

traps.reason: A great mind, but known for science or psychology rather than ethics.
That is the job or the school. Name a person.
A poet first. Wise, but not usually shelved under ethics.

prompts.text: Name an ethical theory, framework or principle.
prompts.flavor: A rule for every choice. Follow any of them far enough down and it leads to the same locked door.
prompts.rules: Any named theory, school, test or principle for deciding what is right, in philosophy or in business.

aliases: Greatest good for the greatest number
Treat others as you would be treated
UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights

answers.lore: Drafted in 1977 by the Reverend Leon Sullivan, a General Motors director, as a code for American firms doing business in apartheid South Africa.
Written in 1932 by Herbert Taylor to save a bankrupt cookware firm: is it the truth, is it fair, will it build goodwill, will it benefit all concerned?
Ancient Egypt's principle of truth, balance and order. The dead had their hearts weighed against her feather to see if they had lived by it.

traps.reason: Too broad. Name one theory or principle.
An economic or political system rather than a theory of right and wrong.
A thought experiment used to test theories, not a theory itself.

prompts.text: Name a company at the centre of a major scandal or collapse.
prompts.flavor: The annual reports were glossy. Hold one to the light and you can still see what was underneath.
prompts.rules: Any company or organisation whose name became shorthand for a scandal, a disaster of its own making or a notorious collapse.

answers.lore: Two Reserve Bank of Australia subsidiaries that pleaded guilty in 2011 to conspiring to bribe foreign officials to win banknote printing contracts.
An Australian firm that sold a pill said to slash fuel use, and sponsored the Sydney Kings and the Western Force. The pill did nothing. It collapsed in 2008.
A Canadian miner worth billions on a gold find in Borneo. In 1997 its samples were found to be salted with gold dust, weeks after its geologist fell from a helicopter.

aliases: Bank of Credit and Commerce International

traps.reason: A government affair or an inquiry rather than a company.
Which one? Name the company.
That is the person. Name the company that went down with them.

prompts.text: Name someone convicted of a major fraud or financial crime.
prompts.flavor: They all had excellent handwriting and steady hands. The sums were perfect, right to the end.
prompts.rules: Anyone convicted of, or who pleaded guilty to, fraud, insider trading or a similar white-collar crime. Surnames alone are fine.

answers.lore: A mining promoter who built a billiard room under a lake. Convicted of fraud in London in 1904, he swallowed cyanide at the court minutes after sentence.
The man who sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap, in 1925, to a dealer too embarrassed to tell the police. He was finally jailed in 1935 for counterfeiting.
He borrowed millions against tanks of salad oil that were mostly seawater with oil floating on top. The 1963 scandal nearly sank American Express.

traps.reason: He fled to Majorca in 1990 and died there in 2001 without ever standing trial.
A jury convicted him in 2006, but he died before sentencing and the conviction was wiped from the record.
She vanished in November 2020, before any criminal charge could be laid.
He died at sea in 1991 before the missing pension millions came to light, so he was never tried.
Charged or wanted, but a fugitive: never convicted in court.
He sold land in Poyais, a country he had invented, but a Paris court acquitted him in 1826.
Jailed over Libor in 2015, but the UK Supreme Court quashed his conviction in 2025.
Fictional, so the court records are thin.
Rich and argued about, but not convicted of a financial crime.
That is the trade. Name someone convicted of it.

prompts.text: Name an unethical or illegal business practice.
prompts.flavor: Each one begins as a small favour, a rounded figure, a thing nobody will check. Each one.
prompts.rules: Any named kind of misconduct in business, finance or the workplace, whether merely shabby or outright criminal.

answers.lore: The tricking or kidnapping of Pacific Islanders to work Queensland's cane fields from the 1860s. About 62,000 came. From 1906 most still there were deported.
Paying workers in tokens good only at the boss's own overpriced shop. Britain's Truck Acts began outlawing it in 1831.
Shaving slivers of silver from the edges of coins. It is why coins have milled edges, and in England it was once punished as treason.

traps.reason: Legal, and usually ethical. It turns sour only when done dishonestly or unfairly.
A crime, certainly, but not one we think of as a business practice.
Too broad. Name a particular practice.

prompts.text: Name a stakeholder of a business.
prompts.flavor: Everyone the firm touches leaves a mark on it. Some of the marks are older than the firm.
prompts.rules: Any person, group or body that affects a business or is affected by what it does.

answers.lore: In 2017 New Zealand made the Whanganui River a legal person with rights of its own, after 140 years of argument by the Whanganui iwi.
G. K. Chesterton called tradition the democracy of the dead: giving a vote to our ancestors, the most obscure of all classes.

traps.reason: Something a business has or makes, not somebody with a stake in it.
Too broad. Name a particular group.
Close, but that is a theory (or a butcher). Name a group with a stake.

prompts.flavor: The argument sounds perfect. That is how you know something has been taken out of it.
prompts.rules: Any named error of reasoning or rhetorical trick, in English or in Latin.

aliases: We've always done it this way

answers.lore: C. S. Lewis's name for explaining why someone is wrong without first showing that they are. He invented Ezekiel Bulver, aged five, to found it.
Deciding by numbers alone and ignoring what can't be counted. Named for the US defence secretary who measured the Vietnam War in body counts.
Named for a 1952 speech by Mississippi's Noah Sweat, who was firmly for whiskey and firmly against it, depending on what you meant by whiskey.

traps.reason: Not quite. A fallacy is a named flaw in the reasoning itself.
Which one? Give the fallacy its name.
That one is sound reasoning. Name a way reasoning goes wrong.

prompts.text: Name a regulator, watchdog or oversight body.
prompts.flavor: Somebody has to watch. Somebody has to watch them, too, and so on, all the way down.
prompts.rules: Any body, Australian or overseas, whose job is to police business, markets, workplaces or public conduct.

aliases: Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre
Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority
Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
Victorian Gambling and Casino Control Commission

answers.answer: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission

aliases: Office of the Gene Technology Regulator
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Securities and Exchange Board of India

answers.answer: Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman

answers.lore: An English court that sat in secret under a ceiling painted with stars. Abolished in 1641, its name still means oversight turned into tyranny.
The 1932 to 1934 US Senate inquiry whose grilling of Wall Street's bankers after the Crash led to the laws that created the SEC.
Two magistrates of the Roman Republic who counted the citizens and policed their morals. They could strike a senator off the roll for bad conduct.

traps.reason: One of the watched, not one of the watchers.
Which one? Name the body.
A government service, but it delivers things rather than policing anyone.

prompts.text: Name one of the UN's Sustainable Development Goals.
prompts.flavor: Seventeen promises, made in 2015, due in 2030. The deep keeps count of promises.
prompts.rules: Any of the 17 goals, by its title or its plain meaning.

answers.lore: The last and least remembered of the 17: the promise to actually work together, with money, technology and trade, on the other sixteen.

traps.reason: That is the whole idea. Name one of the seventeen goals.
A fine cause, but it is not the title of one of the seventeen.

prompts.flavor: They saw what was kept in the dark, and said so aloud. The dark has a long memory.
prompts.rules: Anyone who exposed wrongdoing from inside an organisation, or is best known for bringing such secrets to light.

answers.lore: A US health service interviewer who spent years objecting to the Tuskegee syphilis study before taking it to the press in 1972, which ended it.
Shaw and Richard Marven reported their commodore for torturing British prisoners in 1777. Congress answered with America's first whistleblower law the next year.
Told Europe's regulators in 1973 that Hoffmann-La Roche was fixing vitamin prices. They let his name slip, and the Swiss jailed him for espionage.

traps.reason: A reporter who told the story. Name the insider who brought it out.
Which one? Give a name.
That is who the whistle was blown on.

prompts.text: Name a famous thought experiment or moral dilemma.
prompts.flavor: None of it ever happened. People have argued for centuries about what to do in it anyway.
prompts.rules: Any imagined scenario, puzzle or dilemma that thinkers use to test an idea, in ethics, philosophy, science or economics.

answers.answer: If a tree falls in a forest

aliases: Are we living in a simulation
The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas

answers.answer: What is it like to be a bat

aliases: Can God make a stone he cannot lift
Spear at the edge of the universe

answers.lore: Australian philosopher Richard Routley asked in 1973: if the last person alive destroys every living thing, has he done wrong? It helped found environmental ethics.
Two shipwrecked sailors, one plank that holds one. Carneades of Cyrene asked, over 2,000 years ago, whether pushing the other man off is murder.

traps.reason: Which one? Give it its name.
That one was really carried out, sometimes regrettably. Name one that lives only in the mind.

prompts.text: Name a virtue or a vice.
prompts.flavor: Each of us is weighed in the end. It helps to know what goes on which side of the scale.
prompts.rules: Any trait of character counted as a moral strength or a moral failing, including the seven deadly sins.

answers.lore: The monks' "noonday demon", a listless despair of the soul. It was one of eight deadly thoughts before the list was cut to seven and sloth took its place.
Aristotle's virtue of ready wit: the happy middle between the buffoon, who will say anything for a laugh, and the boor, who never laughs at all.

traps.reason: Which one? Name the trait itself.
That is a deed rather than a trait of character. Name what drives it.

prompts.flavor: Written down in 1948 so that nobody could say they had not been told.
prompts.rules: Any right or freedom set out in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights or a later human rights treaty.

aliases: Right to take part in government
Freedom from cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment
Just and favourable conditions of work
Right to marry and found a family
Right to join a trade union
Recognition as a person before the law
Right to use your own language
Protection of moral and material interests

answers.lore: Article 24 of the Universal Declaration: everyone has the right to rest and leisure, including "periodic holidays with pay". Your annual leave is a human right.

traps.reason: Which one? Name the right itself.
Not one the human rights treaties set out, whatever a national constitution may say.
